categories.name: Motor
categories.blurb: The motor is what actually makes the power — the heart of the build. Everything else in the powertrain exists to feed it.
tips: Needs a controller with enough phase amps to drive it
Check mounting — some motors need adapter plates for your bike
A bigger motor only helps if your battery can feed it (see the Powertrain panel)
High-power motors build heat — consider cooling above ~15 kW

categories.name: Controller
categories.blurb: The controller is the brain — it meters power from the battery to the motor and sets how the bike feels.
tips: Voltage range must cover your battery
Match phase amps to your motor — too small chokes it
Some bikes need a wiring harness adapter — check fitment
App and Bluetooth tuning varies a lot by brand

categories.name: Fork
categories.blurb: Front suspension — dictates how the bike handles braking bumps, rocks, and landings.
tips: Axle size and triple-clamp fitment must match your bike
Spring rate should suit your weight — ask the vendor
More travel isn't always better if the geometry suffers

categories.name: Shock
categories.blurb: Rear suspension — traction and comfort over chatter.
tips: Eye-to-eye length and stroke must match stock
Spring rate should suit your weight
Pairs with linkage choice on some bikes

categories.name: Wheels
categories.blurb: Lighter, stronger wheels sharpen handling and acceleration — often the best-feeling upgrade per dollar.
tips: Hub and axle size must match your bike
Check your brake rotor bolt pattern carries over
Spoked vs billet — weight vs strength tradeoff

categories.name: Brakes
categories.blurb: As the bike gets faster, stopping matters more. Bigger rotors and better calipers transform confidence.
tips: Rotor size changes may need a caliper relocation bracket
Match master cylinder to caliper
Pad compound: organic for feel, sintered for bite and life

categories.name: Plastics
categories.blurb: Bodywork — the look of the bike plus roost protection.
tips: Mounting is bike-specific — 'universal' rarely is
Full kits look cleaner than piecing together
Graphics usually sold separately

categories.name: Batteries
categories.blurb: Your fuel tank and your power ceiling. A weak battery chokes even the best motor and controller combo.
tips: Continuous kW rating must meet what your controller pulls — check the Powertrain panel for bottlenecks
Voltage must match your controller's range
Confirm it physically fits your frame — sizes vary a lot
Swappable packs are convenient; fixed packs usually hold more capacity

categories.name: Handlebar
categories.blurb: Your main control point — bend and rise change the whole riding position.
tips: Bar diameter must match your clamps (7/8" vs 1-1/8")
Taller riders usually want more rise
Cut to width if they feel too wide

categories.name: Charger
categories.blurb: Faster charging means less downtime between rides.
tips: Voltage must match your battery exactly
More amps = faster charging, but also more heat
Some fast chargers need 220V for full speed

categories.name: Cockpit
categories.blurb: Grips, throttles, and displays — the details you touch every ride.
tips: Throttle type must match your controller
Lock-on grips stay put; slip-ons are cheaper

categories.name: Cooling
categories.blurb: High-power builds make serious heat. Cooling keeps your motor and controller alive when you're pushing hard.
tips: Mostly needed above ~15 kW or for sustained high load
Check fitment against your specific motor

categories.name: Drivetrain
categories.blurb: Chain or belt and sprockets — how power actually reaches the rear wheel.
tips: Chain pitch must match front and rear sprockets
Gearing changes trade top speed for torque (and vice versa)
Belt drives are quieter but less tolerant of misalignment

categories.name: Electrical
categories.blurb: Dashboards, lights, and wiring that tie the build together.
tips: Check voltage compatibility with your battery
Plug-and-play beats splicing — look for bike-specific kits

categories.name: Guards
categories.blurb: Cheap insurance — frame, rotor, and case protection that pays for itself the first crash.
tips: Bike-specific fitment
Rotor guards need caliper clearance

categories.name: Linkage
categories.blurb: Connects the shock to the swingarm and sets the leverage curve — subtle but noticeable.
tips: Bike-specific fitment — no universal options
Usually chosen alongside the shock

categories.name: Maintenance
categories.blurb: Consumables and shop supplies to keep the build running.
tips: Stock up on what wears: chains, brake pads, tires

categories.name: Foot Pegs
categories.blurb: Wider, sharper pegs mean more control — especially standing up.
tips: Mounts are bike-specific
Titanium saves weight; steel lasts longer

categories.name: Seat
categories.blurb: Where you spend the whole ride — comfort and control.
tips: Tall seats help taller riders; standard keeps footing easy
Gripper covers for aggressive riding, smooth for moving around

categories.name: Street Kit
categories.blurb: Lights, mirrors, and signals for road-legal riding where it's allowed.
tips: Legality varies wildly by state — check yours
Wiring effort ranges from plug-and-play to a full afternoon

categories.name: Swingarm
categories.blurb: A longer swingarm adds straight-line stability at speed.
tips: Axle and linkage fitment are bike-specific
A longer arm usually means a longer chain
Check tire clearance

categories.name: Tires
categories.blurb: Traction. The right tire for your terrain matters more than most upgrades.
tips: Size must match your rims
Soft-terrain, intermediate, and hard-pack tires are very different
DOT-rated if you ride street

categories.name: Titanium Hardware
categories.blurb: Titanium bolt kits and hardware — shed grams and add color to your build.
tips: Match thread pitch and length to your OEM bolts before ordering
Use anti-seize — titanium galls easily
Axle, brake and motor-mount bolts are safety-critical: follow torque specs
Anodized colors vary between batches — order kits together for a match
